variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Event-driven architecture (EDA) organizes a system around events: durable descriptions of facts that have already happened. A producer publishes a fact such as OrderCreated; one or more consumers react later without the producer calling each consumer directly.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Read an event as a contract, not a callback”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Identity
pairs.detail: The producer assigns one id for one distinct fact.
pairs.explanation: The producer assigns one id for one distinct fact. A retry republishes the same identity, allowing consumers to recognize duplicate delivery.

pairs.label: Meaning
pairs.detail: The event type names a fact in past tense.
pairs.explanation: The event type names a fact in past tense. A versioned name or schema gives independently deployed consumers a compatibility boundary.

pairs.label: Subject and order
pairs.detail: An aggregate key such as order-42 identifies the entity whose events require local ordering.
pairs.explanation: An aggregate key such as order-42 identifies the entity whose events require local ordering. Global order is rarely necessary or affordable.

pairs.label: Causation context
pairs.detail: Correlation and causation identifiers connect an asynchronous chain to the user action or prior event that started it.
pairs.explanation: Correlation and causation identifiers connect an asynchronous chain to the user action or prior event that started it.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Core invariantAn accepted business fact has one stable event identity and a durable path from its source of truth to every required consumer.

pairs.label: Decide the command
pairs.detail: Validate CreateOrder, enforce the order invariant, and choose one authoritative order ID while the caller waits.
pairs.explanation: Validate CreateOrder, enforce the order invariant, and choose one authoritative order ID while the caller waits.

pairs.label: Commit state and intent
pairs.detail: Write the order and its OrderCreated outbox record together.
pairs.explanation: Write the order and its OrderCreated outbox record together. Either both commit or neither does.

pairs.label: Publish from the outbox
pairs.detail: A relay sends committed outbox records to the broker.
pairs.explanation: A relay sends committed outbox records to the broker. A crash can cause another send, so the event keeps the same ID.

pairs.label: Apply local effects
pairs.detail: Each consumer records the event ID with its own state change, then acknowledges delivery.
pairs.explanation: Each consumer records the event ID with its own state change, then acknowledges delivery. One slow consumer does not enter checkout latency.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Choose the event shape before choosing a product”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Publish-subscribe
pairs.detail: Each subscription receives a copy of a published event.
pairs.explanation: Each subscription receives a copy of a published event. Use it when independent capabilities react to the same fact and do not require one shared worker queue.

pairs.label: Retained event stream
pairs.detail: Events remain in an ordered log for a retention window.
pairs.explanation: Events remain in an ordered log for a retention window. Consumer groups track positions, enabling catch-up and replay within the ordering scope of a partition.

pairs.label: Event sourcing
pairs.detail: The event sequence is the source of truth for an aggregate, and current state is rebuilt by replay.
pairs.explanation: The event sequence is the source of truth for an aggregate, and current state is rebuilt by replay. This is a persistence model, not a requirement for every event-driven system.

pairs.label: CQRS
pairs.detail: Commands update a write model while queries use a separate read model.
pairs.explanation: Commands update a write model while queries use a separate read model. Events often build projections, but CQRS can exist without event sourcing and adds consistency lag to manage.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Operate lag and recovery as product behavior”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Publication age
pairs.detail: Track the oldest unpublished outbox record and publish failures.
pairs.explanation: Track the oldest unpublished outbox record and publish failures. A healthy broker does not reveal an event stranded before it.

pairs.label: Consumer lag
pairs.detail: Measure both position lag and age of the oldest unprocessed event.
pairs.explanation: Measure both position lag and age of the oldest unprocessed event. A small count can still violate a time-sensitive business deadline.

pairs.label: Failure inventory
pairs.detail: Alert on retry exhaustion and recovery-queue age.
pairs.explanation: Alert on retry exhaustion and recovery-queue age. Preserve event ID, schema, error, attempts, and correlation context.

pairs.label: Effect reconciliation
pairs.detail: Compare accepted orders with required downstream effects.
pairs.explanation: Compare accepted orders with required downstream effects. Transport metrics alone cannot prove that inventory, payment, or notification is correct.
